latin_note: Farmer's OCR renders the final word with a dotless 'ı' ('anıma'); read as 'anima' (soul) (farmer1998:15442).
translation: The maker of the world is a supramundane soul.
translation_note: 'Opifex' (craftsman/maker) renders the Platonic demiurge; 'supermundana anima' names a soul-level principle above the sensible world, per Farmer's note locating the thesis among a set on the world's demiurge (farmer1998:15526).
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch9, from Latin at farmer1998:15442

sources.pico_relation: Farmer identifies this Proclus passage as the source Pico draws on for the thesis

doctrine: Farmer identifies this thesis, together with 22.1 and 22.3, as drawn from Proclus's commentary on the Timaeus (Diehl 1:300), a set Farmer suggests reading alongside 23.2 from Iamblichus on the same theme of the world's craftsman (farmer1998:15526). Steiris reads the thesis as Pico's report, following Porphyry, that the demiurge of the world is to be identified with a soul rather than with a higher hypostasis (steiris2014:465).
context: The thesis belongs to the run of conclusions 'secundum Porphyrium' (farmer1998:15442).
historiography: The only modern discussion located is Steiris (2014), who cites the thesis as evidence of Pico's engagement, via Anaxagoras, with the lower Neoplatonic hypostases of Intellect and Soul (steiris2014:465).

quotations.text: Pico admits that the Demiurge of the world is the supermundane soul

not_established: Whether Pico's own considered view (beyond reporting Porphyry) endorses this demiurge-as-soul reading is not established by the sources consulted.
The content of Proclus's passage (Diehl 1:300) beyond Farmer's bare citation is not established by the sources consulted.
